newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto seeks talks with IMF on loan.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto seeks talks with IMF on loan.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto said on Tuesday she wanted talks soon with the International Monetary Fund on a stalled $600 million standby loan.

"I hope that my team will be able to resume its discussion with the IMF and that the IMF will be aware of the two months of strikes that we have faced and the impact this has had on enforcing measures which the IMF too believes were necessary," she told Reuters in an interview.

The IMF has withheld payment of an $80 million tranche of the standby loan, due to have been disbursed in June, pending a review of Pakistan's budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June). The budget aimed to cut the fiscal deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from more than five percent in 1995/96.
The IMF, which has voiced concern about Pakistan's balance of payments position, wants the government to clarify the implications of various post-budget tax concessions.
Bhutto said opposition parties had exploited reaction to what she described as a harsh budget, but said the government had stuck to its guns apart from some "marginal" adjustments.
She said Pakistan had foreign reserves of $1.5 billion, so the delayed IMF tranche was "neither here nor there", but added an accord with the IMF would help attract foreign investment.

"We have a rupee that is freely convertible ... anybody can bring in dollars and anybody can take out dollars and we have no fears about it because we have large reserves, we have good exports and we are bringing down the trade deficit," she said.

Her upbeat assessment of the economy contrasted with generally gloomy business sentiment, prompted by the absence of agreement with the IMF and pressure on the rupee, which was devalued 3.79 percent against the dollar on September 10.

The State (central) Bank of Pakistan issued a statement on Monday denying speculation that foreign currency controls might be imposed. It accused unnamed vested interests of spreading rumours to create panic in the financial markets.
Bhutto said trimming the deficit was the only way to curb inflation, officially put at 9.54 percent in the year to August, though independent economists say the real rate is much higher.
"People are certainly unhappy about prices, but the only way to bring down prices is to narrow the gap between income and expenditure and that is going to take a little time," she said.
"The (budget) measures were unpopular. Nobody likes to pay taxes," she said, adding that tax evaders were resisting her government's efforts to document the economy.
Bhutto said her government had repaid $1 billion of foreign debt, now standing at about $23 billion, since it took power after winning elections in October 1993.
"It's my aim that we should pay back at least $2 billion to $3 billion more of our debt before my term concludes in the next two years, because debt servicing is breaking our back."
The prime minister dismissed as "wild and unsubstantiated" opposition charges that her government was corrupt.
